title: Copper a minimal low-level language with OOP and generics
excerpt: Copper is a BSD-licensed language that aims for minimalism, explicit syntax, and simple object-oriented features as a C replacement.
body:
A minimal language can still feel like a full-featured tool. Copper was created as a drop-in replacement for C, but the spec is small enough that anyone can read it in an afternoon. The author describes the goal as “limited brain power”, so every feature is kept explicit and the standard library stays tiny. The concrete `Point` class shown on the site demonstrates how objects, constructors and method calls look without the overhead of larger ecosystems.

In the next sections you’ll see how Copper’s minimalism shapes its syntax, how common constructs are made explicit, what object orientation looks like with only a handful of keywords, and a brief look at the generic support that the language offers. By the end you’ll have a clear picture of the language’s trade-offs and a ready-to-copy example for your own experiments.

## Minimalism drives simplicity  

Copper’s core philosophy is that a language should be understandable at a glance. The author contrasts it with C, pointing out that every feature in Copper is chosen because it can be expressed in a few lines of code.

The entire language specification fits on a single page, and the BSD-licensed implementation is intentionally small. Because the language is deliberately tiny, the learning curve stays flat; a new user can trace a program from the `main` function to the last method without jumping through layers of abstraction.

The minimal set of keywords also keeps the parser simple. Fewer tokens mean faster compilation and easier debugging. The spec avoids hidden magic such as implicit conversions or automatic memory management, so the behavior of each statement is visible in the source. This transparency is the main trade-off: developers must write a few more lines to achieve what C does with implicit rules, but the resulting code is easier to audit.

## Explicit syntax and common constructs  

Copper leans heavily on explicitness. Every variable declaration, function signature and class member requires a type annotation. There is no type inference that silently decides a type for you; you write `var pt: Point!` and the compiler knows exactly what to expect.

Control flow follows familiar C patterns, `if`, `while`, `for`, but without extra syntactic sugar. Blocks are closed with the keyword `end` instead of a brace, keeping the closing token in the same column as the opening keyword and making nested blocks easy to spot.

A short cheat sheet on the site lists the most common forms:

- `def` for function and method definitions  
- `attr` for class attributes  
- `func` for top-level functions  

The explicit `self` reference inside methods reinforces the object-oriented model without hiding the receiver. Because the language does not provide implicit `this`, the code reads like “self.x = x”, which mirrors the mental model of manual memory manipulation in C while still offering the organization benefits of classes.

## Object orientation with classes and methods  

Even with a tiny core, Copper supports classes, attributes, constructors and methods. The `Point` example from the documentation demonstrates a complete class definition:

```copper
class Point
    attr x: Int
    attr y: Int
    def init(x: Int, y: Int)
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
    end
    def translate(dx: Int, dy: Int)
        self.x += dx
        self.y += dy
    end
end
```

The `init` method acts as a constructor; it receives the initial coordinates and stores them in the explicit `self.x` and `self.y` attributes. The `translate` method mutates the same fields, showing how state changes are expressed directly. In `main` the class is used like this:

```copper
func main: Int
    var pt: Point!
    pt.init(3, 5)
    pt.translate(1, 0)
    println("x = \a, y = \a", pt.x, pt.y)
    return 0
end
```

Notice the `!` after `Point` in the variable declaration. It signals that `pt` holds a reference to an object rather than a value, a small but clear distinction that avoids the hidden pointer semantics common in C. Method calls use plain dot notation, identical to many mainstream languages, so a C programmer can pick it up without relearning call syntax.

## Generics without extra keywords  

The site mentions that Copper also supports generics, even though the example does not show them. Generic support is introduced by adding a type parameter in angle brackets after the class name, for example `class Box<T>`. The same `def` and `attr` keywords are reused; no new syntax is required.

This design keeps the language surface area low while still allowing type-parameterized containers such as lists or maps. Because the generic mechanism reuses existing constructs, the compiler can perform the same explicit type checks that it does for non-generic code, preserving the language’s overall transparency.

## Licensing and community resources  

Copper is released under the BSD license, which permits free use, modification and distribution. The official page provides a single-page spec, a cheat sheet for quick reference, and a minimal standard library that can be imported with `import "std"`. The small footprint of the language makes it attractive for educational settings or for projects that need a low-level language without the baggage of a large ecosystem.

## The takeaway  

Copper shows that a low-level language can stay minimal yet provide full object orientation and generic support. By making every type and block explicit, the language remains easy to read and reason about. The `Point` class example illustrates how a complete class, constructor and method set fit into a handful of lines, giving you a practical template for building larger systems without sacrificing simplicity.
